summary: A 1970 proposal for a simplified Network Control Program protocol by R. Kalin. It suggests a simpler way for hosts to manage network communication. It is a proposal, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 60 proposes a simpler Network Control Program protocol for creating two-way links between processes. It uses crates to make the storage needed for a link predictable.

how does duplex linking simplify protocol
what is the simplified ncp protocol
subtitle: A proposal for an NCP with duplex links and predictable buffer needs.

tldr.problem: The existing proposal for creating connections relied on queues that could grow without a bound and were not guaranteed to be serviced.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 60 proposes duplex links that carry message containers called crates, with link capacity determining the worst-case buffer requirement.
tldr.outcome: RFC 60 is a proposed simplified NCP design; the unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

facts.label: Link buffer requirement
facts.value: Equal to the number of crates in circulation

today: RFC 60 is a proposal for a simplified NCP protocol. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: Duplex Links and Crates
sections.content:
Richard Kalin proposes that all user-to-user connections be bidirectional. Each duplex link connects a pair of sockets and carries crates, which are message containers that travel between the two ends.

The link's capacity is the number of crates in circulation. The RFC says the worst-case buffer requirement is equal to that capacity, so a minimal NCP can predict how much storage a link needs.
sections.plainLanguage: A duplex link carries messages in both directions. Its crates move back and forth, and counting them gives the storage requirement for the link.

sections.title: Creating and Closing a Link
sections.content:
A remote process asks its NCP to listen on a socket. The local process sends an RFDL request over the control link with both socket identifiers. If the remote NCP finds a matching listen, it replies with ACDL and the number of buffers the two ends will use.

To close a link, an NCP removes empty crates and sends DEC to request a matching reduction in remote buffers. If a process has died or cannot close the link, ABEND tells the other NCP to stop transmission and reclaim buffers.
sections.plainLanguage: The process requests a link, and the other NCP confirms it with a buffer count. The NCPs remove crates as they close the link or clean it up after an abnormal end.

sections.title: Optional Recovery and Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC's minimal NCP requires link creation, a user interface to links, and link deletion. It proposes optional extensions for larger hosts, including adding crates with INC and using STOP and LINQ to synchronize a link before retransmitting a message.

The RFC describes these as extensions that require cooperation from the foreign host. It also outlines responses to possible overload, including stopping new input and freeing buffers.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic proposal keeps NCP functions small. Larger hosts could add buffers or use an optional recovery procedure if both ends support it.

references.text: Crocker, S.D., Postel, J., Newkirk, J. and Kraley, M., "Official protocol proffering", RFC 54, June 1970.
